Title: Inline Skating Edges: the Edge Is the Whole Leg, Not the Ankle
Description: Where an inline edge comes from: the whole leg, not the ankle, as a rigid boot holds the ankle still. So there is no joint down there to make an edge with: the whole leg leans, knees bent, weight over the wheels. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby corrects edges the same way: at the knee, driven forward over the toes, never lower down. Where the knee goes, the edge follows. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skating Edges: Beginners Live on the Inside One
Description: Every wheel can roll on three edges: inside, centre, outside. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby describes where each level lives. Beginners and advanced beginners have no notion of an outside edge yet: they are still correcting pronation on the inside edge and hunting for the centre. The centre edge is the first goal; the outside edge is the door to the next level. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: inside edge outside edge inline skating, centre edge rollerblading, inline skating levels, beginner skating pronation

Title: Inline Skating Outside Edge: Knowing You Need It Is Not Holding It
Description: The outside edge is the door to intermediate skating, says ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby, and here is the trap: skaters attack intermediate moves, the forward crossover first of all, before they can hold one. The crossover then happens on a centre edge, which is not a crossover. Knowing the edge is required is not the same skill as producing it on demand. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skating Edges Collapse When You Tire
Description: Edges that are clean at the start of a long skate are not clean at the end. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby names the chain: as the legs tire, the knee bend gets shallow, the weight drifts back, and the skate tips onto its inside edge, pronation arriving with fatigue rather than habit. The posture goes first; the edge follows it down. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: fatigue inline skating technique, long distance rollerblading posture, pronation when tired skating, knee bend endurance skating

Title: Inline Skating Foot Cramps on Long Skates Start at the Edge, Not the Boot
Description: Feet that cramp twenty minutes into a long skate are usually reporting an edge. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby explains the mechanism: a skate tipped onto its inside edge loads the arch, the foot muscles grip the footbed to hold the weight steady, and the sharp cramps follow within fifteen to thirty minutes. The grip is the effect; the edge is where it comes from. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skates Hurting Your Feet? Bend Deeper the Moment They Complain
Description: Why tired knees straighten and hurt your arches on long skates, and the fix. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby's fix on the road is immediate: check your posture throughout the skate, and the moment the feet start to hurt, bend the knees deeper, forward over the toes. A deeper flex brings the weight back over the middle of the skate and eases the pressure on the arch straight away. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: knee bend fix foot pain skating, posture check inline skating, deeper knee flex rollerblading, long skate technique tips

Title: Inline Skating Edge Control Is Endurance Work
Description: How to keep a clean edge over long distances: edge control and leg strength. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby gives distance skaters two jobs: conscious edge control, through single-leg balance and edging drills that align the knee over the middle-to-little toe, and glute and leg strength built through fitness work, so the knee flex survives the miles instead of fading. Title: Inline Skating Wobbles: Four Faults Behind Most Beginner Wobbles
Description: Unexpected wobbles, sore feet, skates tipping inward: ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby traces most beginner trouble to four faults. Skates not done up correctly. Knees bent the wrong way, or not at all. No awareness of where the body is. No awareness of how the weight sits in the footprint. Each has its own fix on this site; the point is to check all four before blaming the skates. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skating One-Foot Glide: Learn the Two-Footed Basics First
Description: The plough stop is taught first for one precise reason: both feet stay on the ground, and no one-leg balance is asked of you. That is why a one-foot glide cannot be a second-session move. The single-leg balance and edging drills ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby sets are edge work for skaters who already roll: they come after the two-footed basics, never instead of them. Title: Inline Skating Stance: There Is a Wrong Way to Bend Your Knees
Description: Bending your knees is the first instruction everyone gets, and ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby lists bending them the wrong way among the most common beginner faults. The wrong way is inward: the knees drift towards each other and the skates tip onto their inside edges. The right way is forward, the knee over the middle-to-little toe, so the bend puts the skate on a clean edge. Illustration generated with AI.
